title: Before the next crisis closes a classroom: the $52 million plan to keep children learning
subtitle: Education | New programmes in Lebanon, Myanmar and South Sudan reserve emergency funding and put local organisations in charge of much of the response.
author: ATHENA

paragraphs.text: Education Cannot Wait has committed $52 million to help more than 300,000 children continue learning in Lebanon, Myanmar and South Sudan, with emergency money set aside before the next disruption occurs. Announced on World Children’s Day, 20 November, the package links classroom support with plans to respond quickly when conditions deteriorate.

The UN fund says more than $5 million can be released against agreed warning signs without requiring a new funding proposal. At least half of the intended learners are girls, and about one in ten are children with disabilities. Those figures describe whom the programmes aim to reach; they are not evidence that children have already returned to school.

The change matters because an education grant must survive the conditions that made it necessary. A child enrolled this month still needs a teacher, an accessible classroom and a way to get there after another displacement. Funding continuity means planning for that interruption while ordinary lessons are still possible.

In South Sudan, a three-year, $23 million programme aims to reach 103,200 learners. Its published plan includes flexible calendars for children from mobile herding communities, support for young mothers returning to class and confidential routes back into education for survivors of wartime sexual violence and children leaving armed groups.

The plan also commits to working with disability organisations on individual classroom adjustments. Save the Children International and the national organisation Universal Network for Knowledge and Empowerment Agency will each manage half the grant; national and local organisations will lead nine of twelve county packages. ECW says 59.3 per cent of funding will go to national and local organisations.

South Sudan’s struggle to keep girls learning long predates this announcement. In Oxfam’s account accompanying a photograph taken in Bahr el Ghazal in August 2011, twelve-year-old Monica described wanting to become a doctor. The organisation documented the expense of schooling and the domestic responsibilities pulling girls away from lessons. That archive records an earlier education project, not a participant in the new grant.

Lebanon’s $13 million programme, co-led by Ana Aqra Association and the International Rescue Committee, aims to support about 59,000 learners over three years. Its plan includes transport, learning materials and accessible water and sanitation facilities at fifty public schools. It also provides for support to young mothers, safe spaces for adolescent girls and individual education plans and assistive devices for children with disabilities.

Refugees are explicitly included: the Lebanon factsheet sets a target of 28 per cent refugee learners, including Syrian and Palestinian children. A further 14 per cent are intended to be internally displaced. These are different populations with different experiences; the programme’s reach should eventually be reported in those terms, rather than compressed into a single total.

The photographs of Syrian children attending classes in Lebanon in November 2013 show an earlier chapter of this work. British aid documentation described children restarting education after fleeing Syria, including pupils in the Bekaa Valley. Those photographs establish neither the present circumstances of the children pictured nor outcomes for the 2026 programme.

A separate account from a social development centre in northern Lebanon documented a sister and brother who had missed a year of school. War Child and UNICEF supported language lessons, art and psychosocial activities there. The historical example shows why a return to learning can involve several forms of support, rather than simply assigning a child a desk.

Myanmar receives $16 million under the new package, intended for nearly 150,000 children and adolescents. ECW says half the intended learners are currently out of school and more than a third have been displaced. National and local organisations will manage or receive most funding across the three programmes.

Local management is a meaningful allocation of responsibility, but the share of money assigned to local organisations cannot establish whether families can influence decisions or challenge exclusion. Those questions require evidence from implementation: accessible complaints channels, transparent selection and reporting that shows who is still missing.

For donors and education authorities, the most useful measures will extend beyond enrolment. Do learners attend regularly, progress in reading and mathematics, and remain in education when another emergency arrives? Are girls returning after pregnancy and children needing individual support actually able to use the services described in the plans?

The package gives those questions a funded starting point. Its promise is that a child’s education will not have to wait for a fresh appeal each time a crisis changes shape. Its achievement must be judged by the learning that continues.
